intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for BLACK built around the French Defence — the most strategically committed answer to 1.e4 there is. Black plays 1...e6 and 2...d5, accepts a cramped position, and then spends the whole game attacking White's pawn chain on the queenside while White attacks Black's on the kingside. It is a fighting, asymmetric opening with real plans for both sides: Black is never merely defending, and the structures repeat so often that the theory pays off quickly. The price is the c8 bishop — every chapter here is also about how to activate it. Built the same way as the companion Caro-Kann, King's Indian, Sicilian, Queen's Gambit, Indian Defenses, English Opening, King's Indian Attack, London System and Colle System encyclopedias: main plans, the tries you'll actually meet, sharp lines, typical mistakes, every line verified move-by-move for legality. Chapter 1: Understanding the French (why ...e6, the pawn chain, the bad bishop, and the two fights). Chapter 2: The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) — the sharpest line in the opening. Chapter 3: The Classical and Steinitz (3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4). Chapter 4: The Tarrasch (3.Nd2 c5). Chapter 5: The Advance Variation (3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Qb6) including the Milner-Barry Gambit. Chapter 6: The Exchange and the Rubinstein. Chapter 7: Traps and Tactics. Every line is completed to fifteen moves for each side with engine-verified top play, and every coach comment is preserved.

studies.title: Study 1.1 — Why the French? The ...e6/...d5 Idea

tree.commentAfter: The French is the most strategically committed answer to 1.e4: Black accepts a cramped position from move two and spends the rest of the game attacking White's centre. It is not a defensive opening — it is a counterattacking one.
THE DEFINING MOVE. It prepares ...d5 and it is the reason the whole opening works — and also the reason for its one permanent problem, the c8 bishop.
White takes the centre. In the French, White almost always ends up with pawns on d4 and e5 — a big, strong-looking chain that Black will attack from the queenside.

The point of ...e6. Black challenges e4 immediately. Notice the difference from the Caro-Kann: here the c8 bishop is already shut in behind the pawn, and finding a home for it is the theme of every chapter in this repertoire.
White defends e4 and develops. 3.Nd2 is the Tarrasch (Ch 4), 3.e5 the Advance (Ch 5) and 3.exd5 the Exchange (Ch 6); 3.Nc3 invites the Winawer or the Classical.
Black develops and adds a second attacker to e4, increasing the pressure on White's centre.
THE ADVANCE. White closes the centre rather than trade, gaining space and fixing the structure. This is the most common response and the one you must understand best.
THE STANDARD RETREAT. The knight goes to d7, where it supports ...c5 — the move that will attack the base of White's chain. Note that the knight does NOT go to e4, where it would be chased away.
White supports e5 and prepares the kingside attack. This is the whole point of the chain: White's space gives White the attack.

THE BREAK, AND THE SOUL OF THE FRENCH. Black attacks d4, the base of White's chain. Every plan in this repertoire starts with this move — the chain cannot be attacked at the front, so it must be attacked at the base.

variations.commentAfter: White develops the bishop BEFORE committing the knight to f3 — the modern treatment of the Classical. The bishop supports d4, covers the c5-square and keeps both knight routes open.
Black develops and adds a third attacker to d4. The whole setup is visible already: ...cxd4, ...Nxd4 and a fight over the e5-pawn.
NOW the knight comes out, defending d4 and preparing Be2/d3 and castling.
Black prepares ...b5, the queenside expansion that is the point of the whole French setup. Without it Black has no play against the e5-chain.
White connects the pieces and prepares to castle long, or to push f4-f5. The queen on d2 also supports the d4-pawn indirectly.
Black starts the pawn roller. The b5-pawn attacks c4 and prepares ...b4, driving the c3-knight away from the defence of d5.
White completes the kingside development, eyeing h7 and preparing to castle.
Black pushes past. This is the standard French decision: the queenside pawns advance and the centre becomes locked, which suits Black's pieces.

tree.commentAfter: White defends d4 and develops.

variations.commentAfter: The immediate release, before ...Nc6. Slightly more committal but equally sound, and it avoids any chance of White winning the d4-pawn outright.
White recaptures with the knight.
Black develops and attacks the knight on d4.
White defends and offers the trade of dark-squared bishops.
Black takes, simplifying towards a structure where White's e5-pawn is fixed and Black's pieces are active.

tree.commentAfter: Black adds a second attacker to d4 and develops. The pressure on d4 is now real, and White must keep defending.

The release. Trading on d4 leaves White with a choice of recaptures, and both of them give Black something to work with.
White recaptures with the knight, keeping the chain intact.

THE ACTIVE DEVELOPING MOVE. The bishop comes to c5, where it attacks the d4-knight and eyes f2. This is the classic French bishop: with the light-squared bishop buried, the dark-squared one must be active.
White defends the knight and prepares to castle long.
Black castles and the fight is joined. White has space on the kingside; Black has a target on d4 and the c-file. Both sides know exactly what to do — which is the honest appeal of the French.

studies.title: Study 1.2 — The Chain and the Two Fights

White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
White closes the centre.
Black attacks the base immediately — the defining move of the opening.

Black develops the knight towards f5, the ideal square. From f5 it attacks d4 and cannot be driven away by pawns.

Black develops the KNIGHT FROM g8 to e7, NOT f6. With White's pawn standing on e5, ...Nf6 just drops the knight to exf6 — the same move-order trap that appeared in the Caro-Kann. From e7 it heads for f5. The N is required in the notation because the b8-knight can also reach e7.
White develops.
Black reroutes the knight to f5, the thematic square — it attacks d4 and g3.
White defends d4 and prepares to castle short.

Black develops the f8-bishop before castling. Note this must come BEFORE ...O-O — with the bishop still on f8 the king has no legal castling move, which is precisely the kind of move-order slip the emit gate exists to catch.

White expands on the queenside, the only space available.

White recaptures with the c-pawn, and the chain is now d4/e5 — one pawn defending the other, and both targets.
The knight arrives on f5, hitting d4 and e3. Black now has four pieces aiming at the same pawn, and White must spend the rest of the game defending it.
White develops and defends d4 from the long diagonal.
Black develops the problem bishop — not to its best square, but to the only square available. This is the French bishop's life.
White develops and prepares to castle.
Black develops and prepares to castle. The position is balanced, and Black's plan is completely clear: pile up on d4, trade pieces, and win the pawn or the endgame.

studies.title: Study 2.1 — The Winawer Main Line: 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3

tree.commentAfter: The Winawer is the sharpest line in the French and the one that punishes passive play most severely. It is also the most theoretically demanding — but the plans are unforgettable.
The French.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
White defends e4. This is what invites the Winawer.

THE WINawER BISHOP. Black pins the c3-knight and, more importantly, prepares to give up the bishop for it — accepting doubled c-pawns in return for the dark squares and a permanently weakened White structure.
White closes the centre and gains space.
The break, attacking d4 as always.

variations.commentAfter: The immediate aggression: White declines to ask the bishop a question and attacks g7 at once.
Black defends g7 with the knight and prepares ...cxd4.
White takes.
Black attacks the queen and opens the h-file.
White grabs the second pawn.
Black takes on d4, and the position is the main line with the bishop still on b4 — arguably even better for Black, since the pin remains.
White finally asks the question, but a move late.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

tree.commentAfter: White asks the bishop a question: trade or retreat. This is the main line.

THE DECISION, AND IT IS THE WHOLE OPENING. Black gives up the bishop for the knight. White's pawns are doubled and the c3-pawn is a long-term weakness — but in return Black gets the dark squares, a free hand on the queenside, and the ability to play against the c3-pawn forever.
White recaptures with the b-pawn. Note that the pawn now on c3 is doubled and cannot be defended by a pawn — it is a permanent target.
Black develops and prepares ...b6 and ...Ba6, the standard plan: trade off the light-squared bishop, which is otherwise the worst piece on the board.

variations.commentAfter: White DECLINES the poisoned-pawn raid with 7.Qg4 and just develops. This is the safe route: White accepts a normal position, keeps the extra space on the kingside, and does not risk the queen on an adventure.
Black re-routes the queen to a safe square and prepares ...c4 and ...Nbc6. With White's queen at home, Black can develop normally.
White completes the kingside development and prepares to castle short.
Black advances the queenside pawns, gaining space and driving the bishop back.
White grabs the pawn with check. This is the tactical point of the whole line: the bishop on d3 was aiming here, and the sacrifice must be met accurately.
Black steps aside. The king is heading for c7 or b8, and White's bishop is now offside.
White retreats the bishop, having won a pawn but lost a tempo.
Black develops the last piece and the position is genuinely balanced — Black's activity is full compensation for the pawn.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

tree.commentAfter: White goes straight for the kingside, the correct plan against the doubled pawns: attack before Black can consolidate.
THE ONLY MOVE. Black must defend g7 and prepare ...cxd4. Any other move loses material.
White takes the pawn. This is the critical moment of the whole Winawer: White has won a pawn, and Black has to prove that the attack and the dark squares are worth it.
Black attacks the queen and opens the h-file for the rook.
White takes the second pawn and the queen escapes to h7.
Black takes on d4, opening the centre while White's queen is offside. Black has a rook on g8 aimed at g2 and a lead in development — full compensation for the two pawns.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

THE RETREAT. Black keeps the bishop on the a5-e1 diagonal, where it pins nothing but still eyes the white king's position. The trade is deferred, not declined — Black will take on c3 later, at a better moment.

White develops.

Black develops the knight, keeping ...c4 and ...Nbc6 in reserve and preparing to castle.
White develops, eyeing h7 and preparing to castle.
Black takes the c3-pawn — the point of the ...Ba5 and ...cxd4 sequence. The chess position is now materially unbalanced and Black's a5-bishop is buried.

White reroutes the knight towards f3 or b3 to cover the queenside entry squares.

White takes the bishop. Now Black has given up the bishop for nothing — but notice the structure: White's a-pawn is doubled and the a5-pawn is weak, and Black has a free hand in the centre.
Black takes the c3-pawn, and now the position is a mess in the best possible way for Black: White has three pawn islands on the queenside and Black has all the play.

Black attacks the queen.
White grabs the second pawn, and the race is on — the same race as the main line, but with a very different structure.

The third route into the Winawer: White trades on d5 and the position becomes symmetrical and quieter. It looks harmless — and it is, but it is also very easy to play for Black.
The French.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
White defends e4.
The Winawer bishop.
White takes on d5, releasing the tension before the chain can form.
Black recaptures with the e-pawn — and note that this solves the bishop problem: the c8 bishop now has the open c8-h3 diagonal.

variations.commentAfter: The alternative: White develops the bishop before the knight, offering the trade immediately.

White brings the knight to e2, keeping f3 free for the bishop.

White castles, and Black follows with ...Be7 and ...O-O. A symmetrical, sound position with nothing to fear.

White connects the pieces and prepares to castle long or short, depending on where Black commits the king.

Black develops and challenges d4, the base of White's position. The game is a race between White's kingside push and Black's queenside expansion.

White castles.
THE BISHOP EMERGES. With ...e6 already played and the pawn gone from e6, the bishop comes to g4 — the French bishop's dream, and the reason Black recaptured with the e-pawn.
White develops and prepares to trade.

The French.

Black challenges it.

THE CLASSICAL. Black develops the knight and attacks e4, keeping the bishop's options open — it may yet go to e7 or b4 depending on how White plays.
White closes the centre.
The standard retreat, supporting ...c5.

Black pushes. The b5-pawn attacks c4 and prepares ...b4.

studies.title: Study 3.2 — The Steinitz: 5.Nce2

The French.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
White defends e4.
The Classical.

The Tarrasch is the most solid and most popular treatment of the French at club level. White develops the knight to d2 to avoid the Winawer pin — and accepts a slightly passive setup in return.
The French.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.

THE TARRASCH MOVE. The knight goes to d2 rather than c3, which keeps the c-pawn free and — crucially — makes the Winawer pin impossible. The cost: the knight is passive on d2 and White's development is slower.
The break, immediately attacking d4. Against the Tarrasch Black must be quick, because White's position is solid and slow.
White takes on d5, releasing the tension.
Black recaptures with the e-pawn. Note that this opens the c8 bishop's diagonal — the Tarrasch is one of the few French lines where the bad bishop is genuinely solved.

White gives a second check along the open e-file.
Black blocks again, and note that the bishop is on its best square anyway.
White takes, and the position is balanced. Black has solved the opening comfortably.

studies.title: Study 6.1 — The Exchange Variation: 3.exd5 exd5

tree.commentAfter: The Exchange Variation is the simplest way to play against the French: White trades on d5 and the position becomes symmetrical. It is not dangerous — it is a long, quiet game where Black's bishop is finally free.
The French.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
White takes, releasing the tension immediately.
Black recaptures with the e-pawn. THE KEY POINT: with the e-pawn gone from e6, the c8 bishop now has the open c8-h3 diagonal. This is the one French line where the 'bad bishop' is not bad at all.
White develops.
Black develops.
White develops and offers the trade of light-squared bishops — trying to take away the one good piece Black has.
Black develops and defends e5, keeping the bishop on its active diagonal.

variations.commentAfter: White PINS the f6-knight instead of the simple 6.O-O. The pin is a real question: if Black unpins with ...Be7, White can take and damage the structure; if Black plays ...Bg4, the position becomes a genuine fight.
Black breaks the pin by attacking the c3-knight, a standard and effective antidote.
White defends c3 and connects the pieces, accepting the exchange of light pieces.
Black retreats the bishop, having gained a tempo on the queen.
White castles short, completing the kingside.
Black castles, and both sides are fully developed. The position is a symmetrical Exchange French where Black has solved the pin problem.
White puts the rook on the half-open c-file, the standard plan in the Exchange.
Black reinforces d5 and prepares ...Bf5 or ...Bg4. The game is a long positional fight with genuine equality — which is the honest verdict on the Exchange Variation.

studies.title: Study 7.1 — Traps and Tactics: The ...Qa5+ Motif in the Winawer

tree.commentAfter: The tactics chapter. Every line here is a motif you must recognise instantly — in the French, more than in any other opening, a single careless move loses on the spot.
The French.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
White defends e4.
The Winawer bishop.
White closes the centre.
The break.

variations.commentAfter: White develops the knight instead of the immediate 5.Bd2. By defending d4 first, White avoids the ...Qa5+ trick altogether — Black has no check because the knight covers nothing on the a5-e1 diagonal but the queen has no target.
Black takes the pawn, the standard French decision.
White recaptures with the QUEEN, which is safe here because Black has no available check.
Black develops with tempo on the queen — the reason White usually avoids this move order.
White moves the queen to a safe square, where it supports d4 and prepares to castle long.

Black develops the g8-knight to e7, NOT f6. White develops the bishop, eyeing h7 and preparing the standard attacking setup.
Black prepares ...Bb7 and ...Ba6, the standard Winawer queenside plan: trade the bad bishop for White's good one.
White castles short, completing development.
Black castles too, connecting the rooks. The position is a normal French middlegame in which the ...Qa5+ motif is no longer available — which is exactly the point this line teaches.
White questions the b4-bishop. The standard Winawer decision: force Black to commit before the middlegame clarifies.
Black trades on c3 rather than retreating, doubling White's pawns and keeping the structure asymmetric — the compensation is that White's queenside pawns are no longer a unit.
White recaptures toward the centre, opening the b-file for the rook.
Black finally strikes at the e5-pawn, the thematic Winawer break. The knight on e7 supports it, so it is no longer a case of the pawn hanging in the air.
White takes, since the e5-pawn cannot survive the break.

Black recaptures with the rook, gaining real activity on the f-file and completing a balanced position: Black has the two bishops in spirit and play down the f-file, White has the central knight on f3.

tree.commentAfter: A common and slightly inaccurate move order. White develops the bishop to d2 instead of asking the b4-bishop a question with a3. It looks natural — and it walks into a motif.
Black takes on d4 immediately, because White's bishop is now committed to d2 and cannot easily defend the queenside.
White counterattacks the c7-square, hoping to win the exchange.

variations.commentAfter: Black must deal with the bishop, which White's Bd2 is attacking down the d2-c3-b4 diagonal. Bxc3 is impossible (the knight has left c3, so it would give the bishop away for nothing), and Ba5 is still on the same diagonal. So the bishop steps to c5, where it is safe and keeps an eye on f2.
White retreats the knight, and Black's bishop is safe on c5.

Black develops the kingside knight and prepares ...O-O. A normal, playable Winawer position, reached without losing a piece — which the previous version of this variation did, by playing Bxc3 onto an empty square.

tree.commentAfter: THE MOTIF. Black takes the bishop WITH CHECK — the bishop on d2 was blocking the b4-e1 diagonal, so removing it exposes the white king. White must recapture and loses the initiative.
White recaptures with the queen.

THE LESSON OF THIS STUDY, STATED PLAINLY: do NOT play ...Qa5 here. It looks natural — it hits the b5-knight and the a2-pawn — but the white queen on d2 simply takes it down the d2-c3-b4-a5 diagonal, which the b5-knight has just vacated. The ...Qa5 motif is real, but it needs that diagonal blocked. Black develops instead, and the point stands: the bishop sacrifice on d2 won a tempo and the dark squares, but it does NOT license a queen sortie into an open diagonal.
